summary: Claude is right that the design conflicts with the requirements, but rewriting the design alone is insufficient: the cancellation code must change, and the API is an additional external contract that must be preserved. No source is explicitly authoritative or newer, so precedence should be decided per conflict: requirements govern business policy, API governs externally observable behavior, and design/code must conform to both.

claims.statement: The design's 30-minute cancellation limit contradicts the requirements and API, which use shipment—not elapsed time—as the cutoff.
evidence: docs/requirements.md:2 — cancellation is allowed at any time before shipment
docs/design.md:2 — cancellation is allowed only within 30 minutes
docs/api.md:2 — cancellation returns 409 once the order has shipped and otherwise cancels

claims.statement: The implemented canCancel function violates the shipment-based contract because it rejects unshipped orders older than 30 minutes and can approve recently placed orders without checking whether they shipped.
evidence: src/orders.js:1-2 — canCancel returns only the result of an elapsed-time comparison

claims.statement: The cancellation conflict has high impact because it can wrongly deny valid cancellations and expose authorization inconsistent with the documented 409 behavior.
The requirements and API should jointly win the cancellation conflict because they agree on the business boundary and observable endpoint behavior, requiring changes to both design and code.
The Friday-only refund batch contradicts the requirement that every refund be issued within three business days of cancellation.
evidence: docs/requirements.md:3 — refunds are issued within 3 business days
docs/design.md:3 — refunds are batched every Friday

claims.statement: The refund conflict has high impact because a cancellation early in the week or just after a Friday batch can exceed the three-business-day deadline.

The refund requirement should win because it states a measurable customer-facing deadline, while weekly batching is an implementation choice that must be scheduled or supplemented to satisfy that deadline.
The design's shipment-and-delivery-only email policy contradicts the requirement to email customers for every status change.
evidence: docs/requirements.md:4 — customers must receive an email for every status change
docs/design.md:4 — emails are sent only on shipment or delivery

claims.statement: The email conflict has high impact because customers will miss notifications for every status transition other than shipment and delivery.
The email requirement should win because it is an explicit mandatory customer outcome and the design supplies no exception or competing external contract.
Deleting orders after two years contradicts the seven-year retention requirement.
evidence: docs/requirements.md:5 — order history is kept for 7 years for audit
docs/design.md:5 — orders older than 2 years are deleted nightly

claims.statement: The two-year deletion policy also conflicts operationally with the API's stated ability to return orders as old as seven years.
evidence: docs/api.md:3 — GET /orders?since=... returns orders up to 7 years old
docs/design.md:5 — records older than 2 years are deleted

claims.statement: The retention conflict has high impact because it creates a five-year audit-data gap and prevents retrieval of records that the API appears to promise.

The requirements and API should win the retention conflict because audit retention is the stated business purpose and API availability is externally observable, whereas storage savings is only an implementation rationale.

The API webhook requirement does not contradict the email requirement because they specify separate notification channels, so every-change webhooks and every-change customer emails should both be retained.
The scoped source implements only cancellation eligibility and contains no implementation for refunds, emails, retention, routes, or webhooks.
evidence: src/orders.js:1-3 — the complete file contains only canCancel

claims.statement: If src/orders.js represents the complete implementation, every documented capability other than the partial cancellation rule is missing rather than merely contradictory.
Repository history provides no recency-based precedence because all four files were introduced in the same commit.
evidence: git log output: requirements, design, API, and code all resolve to commit fddddd7 dated 2026-10-06T21:40:51+08:00

claims.statement: Claude's blanket claim that requirements alone are the source of truth is not established by the inspected material.
evidence: No inspected document declares a precedence hierarchy
git log output shows all sources originated in the same commit
docs/api.md:2-4 defines externally observable behavior not fully restated by the requirements

open_questions: Does “returns orders up to 7 years old” guarantee availability for the full seven-year period, or merely impose a maximum query age? The retention requirement strongly favors the former interpretation.

Is src/orders.js the complete application implementation or only the cancellation module? This determines whether the absent refund, notification, retention, route, and webhook behavior is missing implementation or simply outside the supplied code scope.
Is there an unprovided governance document that explicitly establishes requirements or the API contract as authoritative when they disagree?
